pdf_context: Assessment of Indoor Environmental Quality (IEQ) in university classrooms by periods of the day through discriminant analysis Iasmin Lourenço Niza1, Mateus Pedrosa Braga1, and Evandro Eduardo Broday1* 1 IEQ Lab, Federal University of Technology – Paraná (UTFPR), Rua Doutor Washington Subtil Chueire, 330, Jardim Carvalho, Ponta Grossa, PR, 84017-220, Brazil Abstract. Indoor Environmental Quality (IEQ) is fundamental in any environment, as it directly influences occupants' health, comfort, well-being, and productivity. In educational environments, inadequate conditions can impair cognitive performance and learning. This research aimed to analyze university classrooms located in Southern Brazil, using Discriminant Analysis to classify environmental conditions considering four periods of the day: (1) early morning (7:30–9:59 a.m.), (2) mid/late morning (10:00–11:59 a.m.), (3) early afternoon (12:00–02:59 p.m.), and (4) mid/late afternoon (03:00–05:59 p.m.). This classification will be based on data collected from 150 on-site measurements taken between 2024 and 2025. Data were collected using Aura IEQ Discoverer equipment, which covers the tangible aspects of IEQ, including thermal comfort (operative temperature and relative humidity), visual comfort (illuminance), acoustic comfort (noise), and indoor air quality (carbon dioxide concentration and volatile organic compounds). The results indicated that operative temperature, relative humidity, and CO2 concentration were the variables with the greatest discriminatory power between periods. The discriminant model achieved a 50.7% accuracy rate in classifying environmental variations throughout the day, revealing identifiable temporal patterns in environmental conditions, which can help develop strategies for ventilation, lighting control, pollutant, and noise reduction in educational environments. This information can support the implementation of building management policies that promote greater energy efficiency, thermal and acoustic comfort, and improved air quality. All of these benefits contribute to good indoor conditions for users and also for the building’s sustainability. Keywords. Indoor Environmental Quality, Discriminant Analysis, University Classrooms, IEQ.1 Introduction Nowadays, people spend approximately 80 to 90% of their time performing activities indoors [1]. This raises the issue of Indoor Environmental Quality (IEQ), which aims to investigate the interior of buildings and understand how their conditions impact the health, comfort, productivity, and well-being of users [2]. This investigation is carried out through the analysis of their thermal, lighting, acoustic, and air quality aspects [3]. The literature reports several studies on the impact of IEQ in educational buildings worldwide. In primary schools in England, it was found that the learning process was reduced when the ventilation rate was less than 4 L/s [4]. In the same context, the presence of noise also had a negative impact on test scores [5]. Similarly, in primary and secondary schools in Latvia, learning was impaired due to high CO2 concentrations [6]. At workstations in China, cognitive performance was compromised by increased air temperature [7]. Finally, in an architecture office in Malaysia, users' behavior and concentration were affected by poor lighting [8]. * Corresponding author: broday@utfpr.edu.br To analyze IEQ, numerous statistical methods have been employed, including two-step clustering analysis [9], Bayesian logistic regression [10], and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) [11], among others. Among these techniques, discriminant analysis stands out, which aims to verify the difference between groups in terms of several variables, determining whether they are adequate or inadequate to distinguish these predetermined groups [12]. Niza and Broday [13] applied discriminant analysis to investigate thermal comfort conditions in Brazil using the PMV model and alternative models. Gładyszewska-Fiedoruk and Sulewska [14] verified the thermal comfort sensations of individuals in the same location but under different external and internal temperature conditions. Niza, Mendes da Luz, and Broday [15] investigated the prediction of thermal comfort for men and women inside university classrooms. Given this scenario and recent research, studying the variability of environmental parameters throughout the day in university classrooms may be an important topic, as this information can help elaborate building management policies to promote better IEQ conditions for people. Thus, this study aimed to verify how IEQ aspects differ between periods of the day and which variables have greater discriminatory capacity in Discriminant Analysis. 2 Material and Methods 2.1 Research location and data collection The research was conducted in classrooms at the Federal University of Technology - Paraná, Ponta Grossa Campus, Brazil. The buildings were constructed using ceramic blocks and masonry. Each classroom, measuring 65 m², has a capacity for 42 students and uses natural ventilation as a cooling strategy [16]. The classrooms were selected by convenience, and the collection procedure began after obtaining permission from professors to take measurements at pre-established times. Each measurement was completed in 40 minutes. The data collection period ran from March 2024 to June 2025, resulting in a total of 150 measurements. The times were categorized into four periods, based on class intervals: • Early morning (07:30 a.m. – 09:59 a.m.): 17 measurements. • Mid/late morning (10:00 a.m. – 11:59 a.m.): 59 measurements. • Early afternoon (12:00 p.m. – 02:59 p.m.): 46 measurements. • Mid/late afternoon (03:00 p.m. – 05:59 p.m.): 28 measurements. For this purpose, the parameters of Operative Temperature (°C), Relative Humidity (%), Illuminance (lx), CO2 concentration (ppm), VOCs (ppm), and Noise (dB) were obtained. The data was collected using the Aura IEQ Discoverer® device [17] (Figure 1). Fig. 1. Aura IEQ Discoverer® Equipment. The Aura IEQ Discoverer® device, shaped like a USB memory stick and equipped with various sensors, is designed to be connected to a computer's COM port (serial communication port). At the end of each measurement, data were saved in .txt files. 2.2 Development of discriminant analysis From the .txt files, it was possible to calculate the averages of the measurements. First, the data was processed to eliminate inconsistencies, such as values obtained before the equipment reached stabilization in the measurement environment. Next, the averages for each measurement were calculated using Excel software and then entered into IBM SPSS, version 23, for discriminant statistical analysis. This analysis involved the development of canonical discriminant functions to investigate how periods of the day differ from each other based on environmental parameters: operative temperature (T), relative humidity (RH), illuminance (L), CO2, VOC, and noise (N). In this study, the periods of the day constituted the dependent variable and were categorized into four distinct groups, as shown in Figure 2. Fig. 2. Classification of periods of the day into groups. Next, Wilks' Lambda hypothesis test was applied to verify whether the group means were equal or different. Thus, the following hypotheses were tested: • H0: equality of group means. • H1: at least one group mean is different. Another statistical test performed was Box's M test, which aims to determine whether there is homogeneity in the covariance matrices of the variables between the groups. Thus, the following hypotheses were tested: • H0: covariance matrices are homogeneous. • H1: covariance matrices are not homogeneous. For the formation of discriminant functions, the eigenvalues obtained were also analyzed. They demonstrate how different the groups are. In the analysis, eigenvalues are presented to quantify the degree of separation between groups within each discriminant function. Thus, the greater the difference between eigenvalues and 1, the more significant the variations between groups will be, with these variations being duly explained by the discriminant functions. The statistical significance of the discriminant functions was determined using the chi-square test, which assesses the ability to separate environmental variables into defined groups. Joint evaluations of all functions are performed, revealing that in terms of discrimination, the first function will always be the most important. Operative temperature, relative humidity, illuminance, CO2 concentration, VOCs and noise, as independent variables, are associated with non-standardized coefficients, which are the values used to form discriminant functions. These coefficients are crucial for: • Recognize the coordinates of the group centroids based on the averages and thus validate their characteristics. • Allow the creation of canonical discriminant graphs to visualize the distance between groups within the discriminant space. Additionally, a structure matrix was generated to enhance understanding of how the variables affected the formation of these functions. 3 Results 3.1 Discriminant analysis First, the variable values were organized in Excel and then imported into SPSS to generate descriptive statistics with the corresponding means for each period of the day (Table 1). Although Function 1 is primarily responsible for demonstrating the differences between the analyzed periods (as it is the statistically discriminant function with the most significant separation power), the Structure Matrix reveals the underlying dimensional composition of the data. The asterisks indicate that Function 2 represents a highly relevant dimension, characterized by strong positive correlations with Relative Humidity (r = 0.684) and Temperature (r = 0.650). This grouping shows that rooms that score high on this function tend to be both hot and humid. Function 1 establishes a contrast in opposite directions, demonstrating that the rooms were warmer (0.554) but had low relative humidity (-0.656). Finally, Function 3 shows that the rooms have low CO2 concentrations (-0.760) and better lighting (0.686). This may be due to the effectiveness of natural ventilation, suggesting that the windows are open to take advantage of natural light and, consequently, to renew the air, which keeps CO2 levels lower. This structure generally reveals that variables related to thermal conditions (T, RH) and air quality (CO2) are the primary factors distinguishing the different scenarios investigated. This representation, using a scatter plot, illustrates the behavior of the data. Fig. 3. Centroid of the periods of the day with canonical discriminant functions. The greater the distance between the centroids, the greater the difference in environmental conditions between different periods, indicating that variations occur throughout the day and are influenced by the variables analyzed. On the other hand, when the centroids are close together, similar conditions are observed across time periods, suggesting environmental stability in classrooms. The classification rate for the periods was 50.7%, representing the proportion of cases correctly classified automatically by SPSS, which indicates the discriminatory power of the model. This value reflects the probability of correct classification and the efficiency in forming discriminant functions, i.e., the model has a moderate ability to distinguish between the defined groups. Additionally, the results suggest that the differences between the groups are not very significant. 4 Discussion Through Discriminant Analysis, it was possible to establish discriminant functions capable of understanding how IEQ aspects differ between four periods of the day (early morning, mid-to-late morning, early afternoon, and mid-to-late afternoon) and identify which variables have the greatest discriminatory capacity. The canonical functions consisted of five predictor variables: Operative Temperature (T), Relative Humidity (RH), Illuminance (L), CO2 concentration and Noise (N). The resulting model achieved a classification rate of 50.7%, indicating moderate discriminatory power and suggesting that the differences in environmental conditions between the analyzed periods are not significant. Similar results were observed in the study by Di Loreto et al. [18], albeit in a different context. The authors investigated exclusively acoustic parameters in European churches, relating them to geometric characteristics such as area, height, volume, length, and number of side aisles, to understand which factors influence acoustic properties and how these variables vary between different architectural styles (Baroque, Gothic, Modern, Renaissance, Neoclassical, among others). In this case, the classification rate achieved was 74.7%, a performance superior to that of this research, possibly due to the nature of the parameters evaluated, the typological homogeneity of the buildings analyzed, or the specificity of the analysis objective. More notably, Neale, Kummert, and Bernier [19] achieved a classification accuracy of 90% when analyzing data from 40,000 buildings equipped with smart virtual meters. This greater accuracy can be attributed to the large sample base and the set of variables used, including the width-to-height ratio, geographic location, and building orientation. Thus, the higher performance observed in these studies reinforces that discriminatory capacity is directly related to the type and variability of the variables analyzed, as well as the scope and complexity of the environments investigated. It should be noted that the VOC variable was excluded from the analysis by the software due to its strong multicollinearity with CO2. In general, Temperature, Relative Humidity, and CO2 were confirmed as the main factors distinguishing between the different scenarios, acting as the most relevant discriminators. The discriminant functions were developed to classify and predict which period of the day a given environmental measurement belongs to, based on the values of the analyzed variables. The study has limitations related to its moderate discriminatory capacity, evidenced by the classification rate of 50.7%. This low effectiveness can be attributed to the exclusion of potentially important variables, such as VOCs, which were removed due to multicollinearity, and to the reduced significance of environmental differences between the periods evaluated. In addition, the absence of additional contextual variables restricts the interpretation of the results and limits the generalization of the conclusions. 5 Conclusion This study used Discriminant Analysis to investigate how the tangible variables of Indoor Environmental Quality differ throughout four periods of the day, identifying Operative temperature (T), Relative Humidity (RH), and CO2 concentration as the main discriminating factors. Although functional, the model demonstrated moderate discriminatory power, with a classification success rate of 50.7%. This result suggests that the variations in physical environmental conditions between the analyzed periods were not sufficiently significant to clearly differentiate the groups, indicating that the low variability of the physical variables limited accuracy. Compared to related studies that achieved greater accuracy, the main limitation of this research lies in its modest classification capacity. To improve the analysis and discriminatory power, further investigation is necessary. Therefore, it is recommended that a broader set of predictor variables be incorporated to cover the intangible aspects of IEQ. It is suggested to include variables such as occupants' perceptions of Biophilia and Exterior Views, Personal Control, Cleanliness and Maintenance, Layout and Furnishing, which should be quantified through questionnaires. The inclusion of these subjective dimensions will enable the model to differentiate between times of day based on perceived quality, thereby making the analysis of the built environment more comprehensive.
